transcript.text: Bit of a weird one - my son put the microwave on for 10 minutes with nothing in it by accident. Now there's a horrible smell. Is it broken?

⚠ Stop using this appliance
A burning or hot-plastic smell, smoke, scorching or melting can mean an electrical fault or a fire risk. Stop using it, switch it off and unplug it (or turn it off at the fuse box), and don't run it again — not even as a test — until it has been checked by a qualified engineer. It may be damaged, and because there is now a horrible burning smell after it ran empty for 10 minutes, do not use it again until a qualified microwave engineer has checked it. Running empty can overheat the parts that generate and guide the microwave energy. It can also scorch food residue or the small waveguide cover panel inside the cavity. The smell alone cannot tell us which, but internal high-voltage faults are not safe for an owner to investigate or repair. 1. With it switched off and unplugged, open the door and inspect only the cavity: look for black marks, melted plastic, chipped paint, or a burnt/holed small flat panel on an inside wall or the roof. Do not remove any covers.
2. Remove the glass tray and look for any scorched residue underneath or in the cavity. If there is only loose food debris, it can be cleaned once fully cold; visible burning, damaged coating or a damaged panel supports internal/cavity damage.
3. Check the outside vents for obvious scorching or melted plastic, without dismantling anything. If present, leave it unplugged and arrange assessment promptly. Even if nothing obvious is visible, the length of empty running and the smell mean an engineer should inspect it rather than testing it with water or running it again.

It's turned off at the switch but still plugged in, so I'll unplug it now. When we stopped it there was a bit of smoke coming out of the side vents, and it smelled hot and electrical. Inside it's empty, but there's a brownish mark on the panel on the side wall. Is it safe to keep, or should I just bin it?

⚠ Stop using this appliance
If there are flames or smoke is still coming from it, keep away, don't open the door of an oven, microwave or dryer that is on fire, switch it off at the wall or the fuse box only if you can do that safely, get everyone out and call 999.

There aren't any flames and the smoke has stopped, though the smell is fading but still there 30 minutes later. It's a cheap Bush from Argos, about £60 and 2 years old. Should I just bin it, or is it worth getting looked at?

⚠ Stop using this appliance
I would not spend money having a £60, two-year-old microwave inspected after this. The brown mark on the side-wall panel could be heat damage to the waveguide cover, but the vent smoke means the magnetron/high-voltage or cooling area may also have overheated. Keep it unplugged and do not run it again, even with water in it. An engineer could assess it, but call-out and repair costs will usually be more than a basic replacement microwave, and microwave internal work is not safe as a DIY repair. My practical advice is to replace it and take this one to an electrical recycling point/WEEE collection rather than putting it in household waste. Only keep it if you specifically want a qualified microwave engineer to inspect and declare it safe.

candidates: Overheated microwave high-voltage/cooking components after being run empty (high)
Burnt food residue, cavity coating or waveguide cover (medium)

plan: They asked: "Is it broken?" - answer that first.

Safety: a burning hazard is active. The fixed safety warning is shown separately, do not repeat it. It must not be used again until a qualified engineer has checked it: say that plainly. You may explain the likely cause and suggest checks that are safe with it switched off and unplugged, but never say or imply that a check could make it safe to use, or that they might not need an engineer.
The fault they reported is: "horrible smell after running empty". Keep to it: never describe a symptom, result or state they have not told you.

Stage 1 (broad help): say what could cause this, most likely first, as possibilities rather than certainties, including simple causes (settings, loading, detergent, installation, or normal behaviour) where they fit. Then give the safe checks that best tell those causes apart (most useful and simplest first, usually two to four), each with why it helps and what each result would mean; or, if one question would settle it sooner, ask that. Do not ask for the model number in this reply. Do not tell them to buy, order or replace a part yet.
